I remember people laughing at the choice of Heath Ledger to play the Joker. I think that his version of the Joker will stay as one of his strongest archetype. Every time he tells someone about how he got his "smile" scars, the story is different. We never get a "real" explanation about where he came and how he became the Joker. And this makes his character much more solid than if they had tried to go deeper in his backstory. As much as batman needed an explanation for his life choices (why a bat, why no guns, etc - they went over this in batman begins and it was, IMO, fair enough), he needed to be something impossible to understand. A fascinating character, like Hannibal Lecter, brillant and starkly mad at the same time, and, in the Joker's case, motivated by something easy to *realize *(i.e. chaos), but nearly impossible to understand.

But I digress. This movie was a good movie, not a masterpiece but a really good piece that will stand the trial of time as one of the best batman title. The Joker steals the movie and, in fact, so should do every batman villain after he has his own origin story done. The storyline is revolving quite a lot, maybe a little bit too much too, but it's a minor inconvenience when you get a movie of that overall quality.

Just in case someone here hasn't read about it...

You know the scene where the Joker walks out of the hospital and triggers the bomb, but the explosion doesn't go off completely and he turns and stares at it then jiggles with the detonator?

That was not scripted. Everything behind was supposed to explode as the Joker walks off towards the camera, but something went wrong with the timing. Heath Ledger improvised the looking-back-and-playing-with-the-detonator thing. Everyone ended up being impressed with his improv and that became part of the movie.

I personally like it too - shows the Joker in a more disorganized, chaotic light.

One of my favourite action movies. I love the small touches

  • The Joker, when he gets out of the 18wheeler (after the chase) and kicks his minion and makes faces before walking up to Batman
  • Batman in Asia, glides into the building, starts fighting and there's this bit where he turns to hit an enemy but he's already down. Nolan said in the extras that he never wanted the fights to seem like a 'dance' - Seeing Batman making a 'mistake' like that added believability
  • One of my favourite opening scenes for a movie.- I also like the build up of the confrontation between Batman and The Joker. The soundtrack (Aggressive Expansion) was just perfect. Hans Zimmer is knows how to work it up!
  • I'm so glad Nolan had the balls to do something like this.
The ferry scene gets me every time. However cliche these types of humanity scenes may be, they indirectly ask interesting questions. In this case, who deserves to die?

I love how Batman is on site at a couple of different crime scenes in the movie, gathering clues - (the bank, the apartment.) Doing detective stuff, you know?

The way the Tumber is given its own personality through the onboard AI ("Loiter - INTIMIDATE" and "Goodbye") made me really sad to see it go.

Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard's score is just unreal though, and sort of groundbreaking in a sense. I remember coming out of that first midnight screening feeling like I had just been through a 2 1/2 hour adrenaline rush. The non-stop sense of urgency thoughout his movie as chaotic event after chaotic event unfolds is just masterful. Then that big finale to send us off.

This movie was so great that no sequel ever had a chance at topping it. I'm not sure anything ever will. Batman at its best.

In the scene where Joker is explaining his philosophy to Harvey Dent he says "The thing about chaos is....it's fair." It sounds like he says its fear. But the closed caption it's fair. The Joker preferred chaos because his revenge was dealt out in way he thought was fairest.

That was a suprisingly deep conversation, and if taken out of context, or applied to real life, it's very true. He made a lot of sense with those words and I'd like to think that Christopher and Jonathan Nolan sat down with Heath and tried to explain to him that this is what he would be like, if he was living in the real world. He's actually making the most sense in the movie if the world and it's structure was really a big joke.

This is my favorite superhero movie to date, for the sole fact that it is not a superhero film. I'm a huge fan of the pseudo-realism that Nolan tried to put into his Batman Trilogy, and I feel that it reached it's peak with The Dark Knight.
